dialectic: method of reasoning through questions and answers to reach truth
abstractions: general ideas considered apart from particular concrete things
phenomena: observable events, appearances, or things as they are perceived
polity: a particular form or constitution of government in a state
oligarchy: government in which power rests with a small wealthy group
oligarch: a member of a small ruling group that holds power in a state
timocracy: government ruled by men who value honour and military glory
tyrant: a ruler who seizes power illegally and governs harshly
tyranny: rule by a harsh ruler who seized power without lawful right
aristocracy: government by a small class of the best or noblest citizens
democracy: government in which ordinary citizens hold power, often by voting
gymnastic: relating to physical training, exercise, and bodily discipline
guardians: the trained class charged with protecting and governing the ideal city
cobbler: a mender of shoes; a shoemaker
spindle: a rotating rod used for spinning thread; here a cosmic symbol
rhetoric: the art of persuasive speaking, often used to win arguments
mythology: traditional stories about gods and heroes, often not literally true
imitative: representing or copying other things, as in poetry and painting
allegory: a story whose characters and events stand for hidden meanings
parable: a short story teaching a moral lesson through comparison
irony: saying one thing while meaning the opposite, often mockingly
paradox: a statement that seems contradictory yet may contain truth
hypotheses: assumptions accepted as starting points for further reasoning
analogy: a comparison showing that two different things share a likeness
legislator: a person who makes or frames the laws of a state
physician: a doctor who treats illness and cares for bodily health
mathematician: a person skilled in or studying numbers, shapes, and quantities
geometry: the branch of mathematics dealing with shapes, lines, and space
astronomy: the study of the stars, planets, and movements of heavenly bodies
metaphysical: concerning reality beyond the physical world, such as first principles
ethics: the study of right conduct and the good character of people
morality: the principles that distinguish right conduct from wrong conduct
prose: ordinary written language without the rhythm and metre of verse
eternal: lasting forever, without beginning or end in time
contemplation: deep, quiet, thoughtful consideration of truths or ideas
husbandman: a farmer who works the land and tends crops and animals
temperance: self-control and moderation in appetites, pleasures and desires
pilot: the steersman who guides a ship safely through the water
drones: idle members of a hive or society who do no useful work
cubed: multiplied three times by itself, raised to the third power
squared: multiplied by itself, raised to the second power
solids: three-dimensional geometric figures having length, breadth and depth
ratio: a fixed proportional relation between two quantities or numbers
intervals: the distances or gaps between musical notes or pitches
unity: the state of being one whole, undivided, or in harmony
forms: in Plato's thought, eternal ideal patterns behind visible things
tragedy: serious drama showing the suffering and downfall of a hero
festival: a public religious celebration held in honour of a god
prophets: people who claim to speak for the gods or foretell the future
sacrifices: offerings of animals or goods made to gods in worship
impiety: lack of reverence or respect towards the gods and sacred things
ascribed: attributed or assigned to someone as their characteristic
universals: general concepts that apply to many particular things at once
exile: forced removal from one's homeland as a punishment
disciples: devoted students or followers who learn from a master teacher
illusion: a false appearance or mistaken impression of the senses
imitator: one who copies or represents another person or thing
ideal: a perfect model or standard that real things can only approach
sophists: paid teachers of argument who taught clever but often deceptive reasoning
sensible: reasonable, prudent, or capable of being perceived by the senses
scale: an ordered series of musical notes rising from low to high
chiefly: mainly, for the most part, above all other considerations
pursuit: an occupation, activity, or line of work followed by a person
partan: the crab, a sea creature used as a metaphor for lowly things
omnipotent: having unlimited power over all things in the world
harmonies: agreeable combinations of musical notes sounding together
intermediate: lying between two extremes, levels, or stages
sophistry: clever but misleading argument intended to deceive the listener
